conservative.headline: Mission Accomplished: Trump Does What Decades of Presidents Refused to Do — Decapitate Iran's Terror Regime
conservative.byline: As seen on Fox News, Breitbart, CBS News
paragraphs: For 45 years, Iran's Islamic Republic held the world hostage — sponsoring terrorism from Beirut to Baghdad, building nuclear weapons in defiance of the international community, and chanting 'Death to America' while its proxies killed U.S. soldiers across the Middle East. On February 28, 2026, Donald Trump ended it.

In an eight-minute video posted to Truth Social, President Trump announced that "the United States military began major combat operations in Iran" — a joint operation with Israel codenamed "Operation Epic Fury." Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, the 86-year-old tyrant who had ruled Iran since 1989, was confirmed killed in an airstrike on his Tehran compound. Trump told the Iranian people directly: "When we are finished, take over your government. It will be yours to take. This will be probably your only chance for generations."

Sen. Lindsey Graham put it plainly: "The end of the largest state sponsor of terrorism is upon us. God bless President Trump, our military and our allies in Israel." Graham called the strikes "necessary" and "long justified" after years of Iran funding Hamas, Hezbollah, and the Houthi terrorists who attacked U.S. ships in the Red Sea. Even Democrat Sen. John Fetterman broke with his party: "President Trump has been willing to do what's right and necessary to produce real peace in the region."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was equally clear about the mission: "Our joint operation will create the conditions for the brave Iranian people to take their fate into their own hands." Videos quickly emerged from cities across Iran — Karaj, Shiraz, Isfahan, Sanandaj — showing ordinary Iranians celebrating in the streets. These are not the actions of a people who support their regime. They are the actions of a people who have been waiting generations to be free.

The strikes took out not just Khamenei but key IRGC commanders, the head of Iran's secret nuclear research program, and Iran's military intelligence chief — a decapitation strike that has fundamentally dismantled the regime's command structure. Trump had previously warned Iran to halt its nuclear program. Tehran refused. The results speak for themselves.

Critics who wring their hands over "congressional authorization" need a history lesson. Presidents have used military force hundreds of times without a formal declaration of war — from Korea to Kosovo to Libya. The commander-in-chief has the constitutional authority to protect American interests when the threat is urgent. Iran had crossed every red line. The only question was when, not if.

Donald Trump did in one morning what Barack Obama, George W. Bush, and Bill Clinton spent decades avoiding: he removed the world's most dangerous state sponsor of terrorism. Democrats would rather argue about process than celebrate the liberation of 90 million Iranians from a theocratic dictatorship. History will judge this as one of the boldest and most consequential decisions any American president has ever made.

liberal.headline: Trump's Illegal War: No Vote, No Plan, 148 Schoolgirls Dead — and American Troops Now in the Crosshairs
liberal.byline: As seen on NPR, Al Jazeera, Roll Call
paragraphs: Donald Trump launched a war against a nation of 90 million people — killing its leader, bombing its cities, and hitting an elementary girls' school — without a single vote of Congress, without a plan for what comes next, and with U.S. troops in Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar already under Iranian missile fire.

The strikes on February 28 killed at least 201 civilians — including 148 people at the Shajareh Tayyebeh girls' elementary school in Minab, in southern Iran's Hormozgan province. Iran's own Foreign Minister shared the photos. Nearly 100 more were wounded. This is what "Operation Epic Fury" looks like on the ground. Sen. Bernie Sanders didn't mince words: "This Trump-Netanyahu war is unconstitutional and violates international law. It endangers the lives of U.S. troops and people across the region. We've lived through the lies of Vietnam and Iraq. No more endless wars. Congress must pass a War Powers Resolution immediately."

Sen. Chris Van Hollen was direct: "Trump is lying to the American people as he launches an illegal, regime-change war against Iran." Sen. Tim Kaine, who had a bipartisan War Powers resolution ready but was unable to bring it to a floor vote in time, said: "These strikes are a colossal mistake, and I pray they do not cost our sons and daughters in uniform and at embassies throughout the region their lives. The Senate should immediately return to session and vote on my War Powers Resolution to block the use of U.S. forces in hostilities against Iran."

Sen. Ron Wyden put the stakes bluntly: "Donald Trump is unilaterally dragging us into another costly and deadly war in the Middle East that the American people don't want." He's right. An initial YouGov poll found only 33% of Americans approve of the Iran strikes, while 45% oppose them.

Iran is already striking back. Missiles and drones have targeted U.S. military installations in Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar. A missile strike on the Israeli town of Beit Shemesh killed nine people. A leading Iranian cleric has issued a call for global jihad against the United States and Israel. And this is just Day One — with Sen. Tom Cotton saying the operation could last "weeks, not days."

Trump swept into office promising to end "forever wars." Now he has launched one against a nation twice the size of Texas with no congressional vote, no public debate, and no exit strategy. Rep. Thomas Massie — a Republican — called the strikes "acts of war unauthorized by Congress." NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani captured what millions are thinking: "Bombing cities. Killing civilians. Opening a new theatre of war. Americans do not want this. They do not want another war in pursuit of regime change. They want relief from the affordability crisis. They want peace."

148 girls went to school on Saturday morning and never came home. American troops are now in the crosshairs of Iranian missiles with no end in sight. The American people were never asked. Congress was not consulted. The Constitution requires it — and Trump ignored it. History will remember this day, but not the way the cheerleaders in the Senate think it will.

factcheck.headline: What We Know — and What's Still Unknown — About Trump's War on Iran
paragraphs: The U.S.-Israel strike on Iran is the most consequential American military action since the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Here's what's confirmed, what's contested, and what nobody knows yet.
THE UNDISPUTED FACTS:

✓ The strikes happened on February 28, 2026: The United States and Israel launched a joint military operation — codenamed "Operation Epic Fury" (U.S.) and "Roaring Lion" (Israel) — targeting Iranian military commanders, nuclear research facilities, and senior regime officials, including Supreme Leader Khamenei.

✓ Khamenei was killed: Ali Khamenei, 86, who had ruled Iran since 1989, was confirmed killed in an Israeli airstrike on his Tehran compound. Iranian state media confirmed his death and announced 40 days of national mourning. Multiple senior IRGC commanders and nuclear officials were also killed.

✓ A girls' school was hit: The Shajareh Tayyebeh elementary girls' school in Minab, Hormozgan province, was struck during the operation. Iranian and international reports put the death toll at 148, with nearly 100 wounded. Iran's Foreign Minister publicly shared photos of the destroyed school. It is not confirmed whether the school was struck by a U.S. or Israeli munition.

✓ Total civilian death toll: At least 201 civilians have been reported killed in Iran, according to the U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA). Iran's Red Crescent cited 201 killed and more than 700 injured as of Saturday evening.

✓ Iran struck back: Iran launched missiles and drones at U.S. military installations in Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar, and at Israel. Nine people were killed in Beit Shemesh, Israel. The Iranian counterstrikes are ongoing as of March 1.

✓ No congressional authorization was sought or obtained: Trump did not consult Congress before the strikes. The War Powers Resolution of 1973 requires the president to notify Congress within 48 hours of committing forces to hostilities and limits unauthorized military action to 60 days without congressional approval.

✓ Multiple war powers resolutions are pending: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) co-sponsor a House war powers resolution. Sen. Tim Kaine filed a bipartisan Senate version. House Democrats are expected to force a vote this week.
CONSERVATIVE SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: "Previous presidents have done this too — no declaration of war needed" — Partly true but misleading. Presidents have used military force without formal declarations of war, but the scale and stated goal of this operation — regime change in a nation of 90 million — is categorically different from a limited strike. A targeted killing or brief air campaign is legally distinct from Trump's own words: "the United States military began major combat operations in Iran." The president himself called it a "war."

⚠️ Claim: "Iran kept building nukes despite Trump's earlier warnings" — Contradicted by Trump's own prior statements. In a previous address, Trump claimed Iran's nuclear program had been "obliterated." Now his administration is citing the nuclear program as the justification for war. Both cannot be fully true simultaneously.

✓ Fair Point: Iran is the world's largest state sponsor of terrorism by most assessments, having funded Hamas, Hezbollah, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and Houthi attacks on international shipping. The IRGC has directly organized attacks that have killed American service members. The security argument for degrading Iranian capabilities is legitimate and held across both parties for decades.
LIBERAL SPIN VS. REALITY:

⚠️ Claim: "This is exactly like the Iraq War" — Too early to say. The Iraq War analogy is emotionally powerful but not perfectly applicable. Iran's regime is more universally recognized as a threat actor than Saddam Hussein's Iraq was in 2003, and the intelligence on Iran's nuclear program is not comparable to the WMD claims. The parallel is more apt regarding regime change and the absence of an exit strategy.

⚠️ Claim: "Trump killed 148 schoolgirls" — The school was struck; 148 people died. But it has not been confirmed whether the strike was executed by U.S. or Israeli forces, what the intended target was, or whether the school was being used for military purposes. These details matter legally and morally, even if the civilian death toll is horrifying regardless.

✓ Fair Point: An initial YouGov poll found only 33% of Americans approve of the strikes, with 45% opposed. The war was launched without congressional authorization in clear tension with the War Powers Act. Trump is simultaneously asking Americans to accept that their sons and daughters "may be lost" in a war that was never debated or voted on by their elected representatives.
THE BIGGER PICTURE:

The operation marks the second time in eight months that the Trump administration has launched strikes on Iran — the first having been framed as limited and targeted. This time, the stated goal is regime change. Whether that goal is achievable militarily, and at what cost, is a question no one in Washington has yet answered publicly.

Section 5(b) of the War Powers Resolution gives Congress the power to require withdrawal of U.S. forces within 60 days if no authorization is passed. Both the Massie-Khanna House resolution and the Kaine Senate resolution are expected to come to a floor vote within days — but passage requires peeling off enough Republicans, and Senate Majority Leader Thune has not yet said he will allow a vote.

The Bottom Line: A 45-year-old theocracy that bankrolled global terrorism is gone. So are 148 girls who showed up to school on a Saturday morning. Both of those sentences are true. Whether the first justifies the second — and whether the president of the United States had the constitutional authority to make that call alone — is the defining question of this moment. Congress was designed to answer it. So far, it hasn't been asked.
